description: 1. Wrap several small plastic animals loosely in aluminum foil. 2. Place the 'silver rocks' in a bowl. 3. Encourage the child to use both hands to pull and tear the foil away to discover the animal inside.
activity_photo: [Image: Child tearing foil off a toy dinosaur]

description: 1. Cut a narrow slit in the plastic lid of an old coffee can or yogurt tub. 2. Give the child a deck of playing cards. 3. Show them how to orient the card horizontally and push it through the slit.
toy_photo: [Image: Plastic tub with a slit in the lid]
activity_photo: [Image: Child sliding a playing card into a slot]

description: 1. Roll out several small balls of playdough on a sturdy table. 2. Give the child a lightweight wooden or plastic toy mallet. 3. Encourage them to raise the mallet and smash the playdough flat, engaging their shoulder muscles.
activity_photo: [Image: Child swinging a toy hammer at playdough]

description: 1. Set up a basin of water and a few floating toys (like rubber ducks). 2. Give the child a plastic turkey baster. 3. Show them how to squeeze the bulb to suck up water, and squeeze it again to squirt the ducks.
tools: Turkey baster, water basin, floating toys
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing a baster to squirt water]

description: 1. Provide a wooden toy fruit set held together by Velcro. 2. Show the child how to hold the fruit with one hand and the wooden 'knife' with the other. 3. Encourage them to saw through the Velcro to 'cut' the fruit.
toy_photo: [Image: Wooden apple sliced in half with velcro]
activity_photo: [Image: Child using a wooden knife on a toy fruit]

description: 1. Provide an empty sandwich bag with a sliding zipper. 2. Have the child hold the bag steady. 3. Show them how to pinch the plastic slider and pull it from one side to the other to close the bag.
toy_photo: [Image: Plastic bag with a red slider zip]
activity_photo: [Image: Child's fingers pinching a ziploc slider]

description: 1. Place a large, empty cardboard box on its side. 2. Give the child thick markers or crayons. 3. Have the child lie on their tummy inside the box and color on the 'walls' and 'ceiling'.
activity_photo: [Image: Child lying inside a box drawing on the walls]

description: 1. Crack a few thick, child-safe glow sticks to activate them. 2. Dim the bathroom lights and drop the glow sticks into the bathwater. 3. Let the child splash and reach for the illuminated colors under the water.
activity_photo: [Image: Child playing in a dark tub lit by glow sticks]

description: 1. Tape a long sheet of large-pocket bubble wrap to the floor. 2. Take off the child's shoes. 3. Encourage them to run, jump, and stomp on the sheet to hear and feel the loud pops beneath their feet.
activity_photo: [Image: Child jumping with both feet on bubble wrap]

description: 1. Snap the very top stem off a banana to create a starting edge. 2. Hand the banana to the child. 3. Instruct them to pinch the edge and pull down to peel the fruit themselves for a snack.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling the peel down a banana]

description: 1. Boil flaxseeds in water and strain to create a taste-safe, slimy gel. 2. Place the cooled slime in a tray with small waterproof toys. 3. Encourage the child to plunge their hands in and explore the gooey, slippery texture.
activity_photo: [Image: Child's hands covered in taste-safe slime]

description: 1. Lay out a photo of a shoe, a spoon, and a ball. 2. Hand the child the physical shoe, spoon, and ball. 3. Ask them to place the real object on top of the matching photograph.
toy_photo: [Image: Photo of a shoe next to a real shoe]
activity_photo: [Image: Child placing a spoon on its matching picture]

description: 1. Loosely tie several thick satin ribbons around the rungs of a chair or a baby gate. 2. Leave the ends dangling. 3. Show the child how to pull the ends to untie the knots and free the ribbons.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling a ribbon knot apart]

description: 1. Sit facing the child. 2. Say their name slowly, emphasizing the syllables (e.g., 'E-li-jah'). 3. Clap your hands once for each syllable and encourage the child to clap along with the sounds of their name.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent and child clapping to words]

description: 1. Stand facing a wall with the child, placing hands on the wall for balance. 2. Demonstrate stepping one foot to the side, then bringing the other foot to meet it. 3. Encourage them to 'crab walk' sideways down the hallway.
activity_photo: [Image: Child side-stepping along a wall]

description: 1. Stand facing the child and hold both of their hands firmly. 2. Lift one of your feet like a flamingo. 3. Say 'Lift!' and help them shift their weight to balance on one foot for 2 to 3 seconds.
activity_photo: [Image: Child standing on one foot while holding parent's hands]

description: 1. Take a lightweight play scarf and scrunch it into a ball. 2. Throw it lightly into the air directly above the child. 3. As the scarf slowly floats down, encourage the child to reach out and grab it before it hits the floor.
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching up to catch a falling scarf]

description: 1. Prop up a long piece of cardboard on a low sofa to create a simple ramp. 2. Sit the infant near the bottom. 3. Roll a brightly colored car down the ramp so their eyes track the fast movement from top to bottom.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant watching a car roll down a cardboard ramp]

description: 1. Hand the infant two light, wooden or plastic blocks, one in each hand. 2. Demonstrate banging your own hands together. 3. Encourage the infant to bring both hands to the midline to smash the blocks together to make noise.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant holding two blocks together]

description: 1. Set up a cup of water and an empty ice cube tray. 2. Give the child a large plastic pipette or medicine dropper. 3. Show them how to pinch the top to get water, and squeeze it to release drops into the individual tray slots.
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing water drops into a tray]

description: 1. Gather items like sandpaper, a loofah, a smooth block, and a silk cloth. 2. Set out two bowls. 3. Have the child feel each item and help them place the 'scratchy' things in one bowl and the 'soft/smooth' things in the other.
toy_photo: [Image: Square of sandpaper and a smooth stone]
activity_photo: [Image: Child touching sandpaper thoughtfully]

description: 1. Take three rectangular blocks. 2. Stand two blocks up vertically with a gap between them. 3. Show the child how to balance the third block horizontally across the top to create a bridge, then let them try.
activity_photo: [Image: Child balancing a block to make a bridge]

description: 1. Show the child how to place square blocks side-by-side in a straight line on the floor. 2. Make a 'Choo-choo' sound. 3. Encourage the child to add more blocks to make the train as long as possible.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing blocks together in a line]

description: 1. Draw several large circles on the driveway with chalk. 2. Call out 'Jump to the blue circle!'. 3. Have the child leap or step into the corresponding circle to practice targeting and color recognition.
activity_photo: [Image: Child jumping into a chalk circle]

description: 1. Scatter dry, crunchy leaves on the grass or a patio. 2. Give the child a pair of large plastic tongs. 3. Have them squeeze the tongs to pick up the leaves and transfer them into a bucket.
activity_photo: [Image: Child using tongs to grab a leaf]

description: 1. Fill a basin with soapy water and provide a toothbrush or small sponge. 2. Drop in a few plastic toy cars. 3. Show the child how to scrub the 'dirt' off the cars and rinse them in a second bin of clean water.
toy_photo: [Image: Plastic toy car covered in suds]
activity_photo: [Image: Child scrubbing a toy car with a sponge]

description: 1. Provide a thick block of craft styrofoam. 2. Give the child several large plastic golf tees and a wooden toy hammer. 3. Show them how to hold the tee with one hand and tap it into the foam with the hammer using the other.
tools: Styrofoam block, plastic golf tees, toy hammer
activity_photo: [Image: Child hammering a tee into styrofoam]

description: 1. Fill a large baking dish with dry rolled oats. 2. Give the child measuring cups and spoons. 3. Allow them to freely scoop, pour, and transfer the oats between containers to practice wrist rotation.
tools: Dry oats, measuring cups, baking dish
activity_photo: [Image: Child pouring dry oats from a cup]

description: 1. Give the child a few large leaves of washed romaine or iceberg lettuce. 2. Set a clean salad bowl in front of them. 3. Show them how to pinch and pull hands in opposite directions to tear the lettuce into small pieces for a meal.
activity_photo: [Image: Child tearing a piece of lettuce in half]

description: 1. Present a set of large, easy-to-open wooden nesting dolls. 2. Show the child how to grip the top and bottom. 3. Help them apply a twisting and pulling motion to pop the doll open and find the smaller one inside.
activity_photo: [Image: Child twisting a nesting doll open]

description: 1. Provide a sheet of gel window clings (large shapes only). 2. Have the child peel a shape off the plastic backing. 3. Encourage them to press it flat against a glass window or sliding door.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pressing a gel sticker onto a window]

description: 1. Place three toy animals (e.g., pig, horse, duck) in front of the child. 2. Make the sound of one animal clearly ('Oink, oink'). 3. Ask the child to hand you the animal that makes that sound.
activity_photo: [Image: Child holding up a toy pig]

description: 1. Lay a small blanket flat on the floor. 2. Place a desired toy on the far end of the blanket, out of the child's reach. 3. Encourage the child to pull the fabric of the blanket toward them to bring the toy closer.
toy_photo: [Image: Toy sitting on a baby blanket]
activity_photo: [Image: Infant pulling a blanket to get a toy]

description: 1. Fill a clear cup with water or a smoothie. 2. Insert a long, looped 'silly straw'. 3. Have the child suck strongly to draw the liquid up through the loops, observing the liquid travel while building cheek and lip strength.
activity_photo: [Image: Child drinking hard through a curly straw]

description: 1. 'Hide' plastic animals in mud or shaving cream. 2. Provide a tub of warm water and a small towel. 3. Have the child dunk the animals, wash them clean, and dry them off individually.
tools: Plastic animals, mud/shaving cream, water tub
toy_photo: [Image: Plastic animals covered in shaving foam]
activity_photo: [Image: Child rinsing a toy animal in water]

description: 1. Take the cushions off the sofa and scatter them unevenly on the floor. 2. Sit at the other side of the 'mountain' with a toy. 3. Encourage the infant to crawl over the highly unstable, squishy surfaces, demanding intense core engagement.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant struggling happily to climb over a cushion]

description: 1. Hang a balloon from a doorway so it hovers about a foot off the floor. 2. Have the child lie flat on their back underneath it. 3. Encourage them to lift both legs simultaneously to kick the balloon.
activity_photo: [Image: Child on back kicking up at a balloon]

description: 1. Provide a wooden 'busy board' featuring various locks, latches, and sliding bolts. 2. Demonstrate how to slide a bolt or unhook a latch. 3. Let the child experiment with pinching and sliding the hardware to open the doors.
activity_photo: [Image: Child focusing on unlocking a metal latch]

description: 1. Fill a large pot with water and toss in several large pom-poms or ping-pong balls. 2. Give the child a deep soup ladle. 3. Have them fish the floating items out of the water and transfer them to a dry bowl.
activity_photo: [Image: Child scooping a ping pong ball out of water]

description: 1. Give the child a cardboard box large enough to sit in. 2. Give them a plastic plate to use as a 'steering wheel'. 3. Encourage them to sit inside, turn the wheel, and make 'Vroom' noises as they pretend to drive.
activity_photo: [Image: Child sitting in a box holding a plate like a wheel]

description: 1. Roll up a hand towel into a thick rope. 2. Have the child grab one end while you grab the other. 3. Initiate a very gentle game of tug-of-war, letting the child pull against your resistance.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling hard on a towel held by parent]

description: 1. Place a toy drum in front of the child. 2. Say a word like 'Ap-ple'. 3. Help the child hit the drum twice, mapping the physical strike to the auditory syllables.
activity_photo: [Image: Child hitting a drum twice]

description: 1. Provide a shoelace with a hard aglet and a bowl of jumbo wooden beads. 2. Show the child how to hold the bead in one hand and push the lace through with the other. 3. Help them pull it down to create a necklace.
toy_photo: [Image: Jumbo beads with a wide hole]
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing a string through a bead]

description: 1. During bath time, hand the child a soft, water-logged sponge. 2. Hold a plastic cup in front of them. 3. Instruct them to squeeze the sponge as hard as they can to fill the cup with the extracted water.
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing bathwater out of a sponge]

description: 1. Place a few mild stickers on the child's arms, knees, or top of their hands. 2. Say, 'Oh no, there is a sticker on your knee!'. 3. Have the child locate the sticker visually, reach across their body, and peel it off.
activity_photo: [Image: Child peeling a sticker off their own knee]

description: 1. Give the child strips of construction paper. 2. Teach them the 'pinch and pull' method (one thumb facing them, one thumb facing away). 3. Have them rip the strips into tiny squares to use for a later craft.
activity_photo: [Image: Child's hands ripping paper in opposite directions]

description: 1. Place a small piece of fruit (sweet) and a small pretzel (salty) on a plate. 2. Have the child eat the fruit and say 'Sweet!'. 3. Have them eat the pretzel and say 'Salty!', exploring different taste receptors.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to a pretzel]

description: 1. Place the infant on your knees facing you. 2. Sing a song, bouncing them slowly at first. 3. Speed up the song and bounce them faster, helping their inner ear adjust to changing speeds.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent bouncing infant quickly on knees]

description: 1. Provide a piggy bank with a narrow top slot and large plastic coins. 2. Have the child pick up a coin using a pincer grasp. 3. Require them to rotate their wrist to align the coin perfectly with the slot to drop it in.
toy_photo: [Image: Ceramic piggy bank with a slot]
activity_photo: [Image: Child aligning a coin with a slot]

description: 1. Have the child stand facing a solid wall. 2. Tell them to put both palms flat against the wall. 3. Say, 'Try to push the wall over!' and have them lean in and push as hard as they can for 5 seconds.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing against a wall with intense effort]

description: 1. Dip the wheels of a toy plastic car into washable paint. 2. Place a large sheet of paper on the floor. 3. Have the child 'drive' the car across the paper to see the tire tracks form a pattern.
activity_photo: [Image: Child rolling a painted car across paper]

description: 1. Place several ice cubes in a bowl of cold water. 2. Set an empty bowl next to it. 3. Give the child a slotted spoon and ask them to scoop the slippery ice out of the water and transfer it to the empty bowl.
activity_photo: [Image: Child balancing an ice cube on a spoon]

description: 1. Give the child a large, heavy (but manageable) hardcover book. 2. Ask them to hold it with two hands against their chest. 3. Instruct them to carry it across the room to a specific shelf, engaging their core to stabilize the weight.
activity_photo: [Image: Child carrying a heavy book with both hands]

description: 1. Tape a large sheet of paper to a wall at the child's eye level. 2. Give them a crayon. 3. Guide their hand to draw a massive semi-circle from their far left to their far right, crossing the center of their body.
activity_photo: [Image: Child drawing a large arc on a wall]

description: 1. Tell the child you are going to practice inside and outside voices. 2. Whisper, 'Yay,' and have them whisper back. 3. Throw your hands up and shout, 'YAY!' and have them shout back, learning volume control.
activity_photo: [Image: Child shouting with hands in the air]

description: 1. Print a picture of a farm and a picture of an ocean. 2. Provide figures of a cow, a pig, a shark, and a fish. 3. Ask the child to place the farm animals on the farm picture, and the ocean animals on the water.
activity_photo: [Image: Child placing a shark on a blue paper]

description: 1. Stand facing the child in an open hallway. 2. Hold their hands. 3. Tell them to take steps backward while you walk forward toward them, building spatial awareness and coordination.
activity_photo: [Image: Child stepping backward while holding parent]

description: 1. Give the child a block or a toy phone. 2. Hold a block to your own ear and say, 'Ring ring! Hello?'. 3. Pause and wait for the child to put their block to their ear and 'answer' the call.
activity_photo: [Image: Child holding a block to their ear]

description: 1. Provide a sturdy cardboard tube (like from a paper towel roll). 2. Give the child a few thick, colorful rubber bands. 3. Show them how to stretch the band with both hands to wrap it around the tube.
activity_photo: [Image: Child stretching a rubber band over a tube]

description: 1. Sit in front of a mirror with the child. 2. Stick your tongue out as far as it goes, then move it side to side. 3. Encourage the child to copy you, improving tongue coordination for speech development.
activity_photo: [Image: Child sticking their tongue out in a mirror]

description: 1. Fill a cup with water and provide a plastic straw. 2. Instruct the child NOT to drink, but to blow air out. 3. Let them blow into the straw to make a noisy, bubbling volcano, practicing exhalation control.
toy_photo: [Image: Cup of water with a straw]
activity_photo: [Image: Child blowing bubbles into a cup]

description: 1. Take the child to a playground with a low pull-up bar or monkey bar. 2. Lift them so they can grip the bar. 3. Support their hips slightly and let them hang by their hands for 3-5 seconds to build grip and core strength.
activity_photo: [Image: Child hanging from a bar with parent supporting]

description: 1. Put a few heavy books in a plastic laundry basket. 2. Set it on a smooth floor. 3. Encourage the child to put their hands on the side and push the heavy basket across the room.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing a weighted basket]

description: 1. Lay a brightly colored string or piece of yarn flat across the floor. 2. Show the child how to stand on one side. 3. Have them jump with both feet over the line without stepping on it.
activity_photo: [Image: Child jumping over a string on the floor]

description: 1. Place several strips of masking tape firmly onto a table. 2. Fold the very end of each strip over to make a tiny tab. 3. Have the child use their thumb and pointer finger to pinch the tab and pull the tape up.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pinching a piece of tape on a table]

description: 1. Place a cotton ball on a table for you and one for the child. 2. Get down to eye level with the table. 3. Tell the child to blow on their cotton ball to race yours across the table to the edge.
activity_photo: [Image: Child blowing a cotton ball across a table]

description: 1. Remove the caps from several thick, washable markers. 2. Mix up the caps and markers. 3. Have the child match the colors and use both hands to firmly push the cap back onto the marker until it clicks.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing a cap onto a marker]

description: 1. Open both ends of a large cardboard box to make a tunnel. 2. Place it on the floor. 3. Encourage the child to crawl through the enclosed space, learning how to lower their head and adjust their body.
activity_photo: [Image: Child crawling inside a box]

description: 1. Find a real spoon, a real cup, and a real shoe. 2. Find a toy spoon, a toy cup, and a doll shoe. 3. Have the child pair the tiny toy versions with their life-sized counterparts.
toy_photo: [Image: Real spoon next to a plastic toy spoon]
activity_photo: [Image: Child matching a toy cup to a real cup]

description: 1. Fill a bin with dry black beans and a few bright yellow pom-poms. 2. Give the child oversized plastic tweezers. 3. Ask them to scan the bin, pinch the tweezers, and extract only the yellow pom-poms.
tools: Bin, black beans, yellow pom-poms, tweezers
activity_photo: [Image: Child using tweezers to pick up a pom-pom]

description: 1. Give the child a small lump of playdough and a clean metal garlic press. 2. Help them place the dough in the chamber. 3. Have them use both hands to squeeze the handles together to make playdough 'hair' come out.
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing a garlic press full of dough]

description: 1. Form a large, solid mound of playdough on the table. 2. Provide a handful of stiff craft feathers. 3. Encourage the child to pinch the base of the feather and stab it downward into the dough.
activity_photo: [Image: Child poking a feather into a ball of dough]

description: 1. Have the child lay flat on a mat. 2. Take a large, soft pillow and press it gently but firmly over their back and legs (never the head). 3. Provide this deep pressure 'squish' for a few seconds to calm their nervous system.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent pressing a pillow gently on a child's back]

description: 1. Go outside in the fall and find a pile of dry, crunchy leaves. 2. Instruct the child to stomp hard on the leaves. 3. Point to your ears and talk about the 'crunch' sound the leaves make when crushed.
activity_photo: [Image: Child stomping on a pile of leaves]

description: 1. Make a batch of simple salt dough or bread dough. 2. Place it on a clean, floured surface. 3. Show the child how to use the heels of both hands to push the dough away, fold it, and push again.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing dough with both hands]

description: 1. Present a jumbo plastic nut and bolt toy that is already screwed together. 2. Hold the bolt steady. 3. Have the child use their other hand to twist the nut counter-clockwise until it comes off completely.
toy_photo: [Image: Large green plastic bolt and nut]
activity_photo: [Image: Child twisting a nut off a bolt]

description: 1. Take a loud, ticking kitchen timer and set it for 1 minute. 2. Hide it under a blanket or behind a chair while the child covers their eyes. 3. Have the child quietly listen and follow the ticking sound to find it.
activity_photo: [Image: Child listening closely to find a hidden timer]

description: 1. Firmly snap two large, interlocking plastic blocks (like Duplo) together. 2. Give the pair to the child. 3. Require them to grip tightly and pull with their arm and chest muscles to separate the pieces.
toy_photo: [Image: Two large plastic blocks stuck together]
activity_photo: [Image: Child straining to pull two blocks apart]

description: 1. Blend a thick smoothie using yogurt and frozen fruit. 2. Serve it in a cup with a standard width straw. 3. The child will have to use intense lip seal and suction power to draw the thick liquid up.
toy_photo: [Image: Cup with a thick pink smoothie]
activity_photo: [Image: Child drinking a thick smoothie through a straw]

description: 1. Take out distinct, safe spices like cinnamon, vanilla extract, and mint. 2. Open one jar and hold it a few inches from the child's nose. 3. Ask them to take a sniff and talk about whether they like or dislike the smell.
toy_photo: [Image: Open jars of cinnamon and mint]
activity_photo: [Image: Child sniffing a spice jar]

description: 1. Have the child lay on their tummy. 2. Lift their legs up by the thighs or hips (not the ankles). 3. Encourage them to 'walk' forward using only their hands, building immense upper body and core stability.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent holding child's legs while child walks on hands]

description: 1. Scribble all over a small chalkboard or whiteboard. 2. Hand the child a dry sponge or eraser. 3. Have them use broad, sweeping arm movements to wipe the board completely clean.
activity_photo: [Image: Child wiping a chalkboard clean]

description: 1. Sit on the floor with your legs spread in a V-shape, facing the child who is sitting the same way. 2. Roll a medium ball smoothly toward them. 3. Encourage them to watch it and trap it with both hands before it hits their tummy.
activity_photo: [Image: Child trapping a rolling ball with both hands]

description: 1. Provide a highly elastic, rubbery sensory toy. 2. Hold one side firmly. 3. Encourage the infant to grab the other side and pull, feeling the resistance and stretch of the material.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant pulling a stretchy toy]

description: 1. Place a bowl of ice cubes next to a bowl of safely warm water. 2. Have the child touch the ice and say 'Cold!'. 3. Quickly have them dip their fingers in the warm water and say 'Warm!', teaching temperature contrasts.
toy_photo: [Image: Bowl of ice and bowl of water]
activity_photo: [Image: Child touching ice then warm water]

description: 1. Stretch a piece of tissue paper tightly over the top of a plastic cup and secure it with a rubber band. 2. Give the child a dull pencil or a blunt wooden skewer. 3. Have them poke holes through the taut paper.
tools: Cup, tissue paper, rubber band, dull pencil
activity_photo: [Image: Child poking a pencil through paper]

description: 1. Shake a rattle continuously. 2. Have the child close their eyes. 3. Walk slowly around the child in a circle, asking them to point to where the sound is coming from as it moves.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing blindly toward a sound]

description: 1. Stick several strips of painter's tape on a wall, slightly above the child's head height. 2. Have them reach up high. 3. Instruct them to grab the tape and pull down hard, using their shoulder and arm strength.
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching high to pull tape off a wall]

description: 1. Present a tiny dab of plain yogurt (sour) and a tiny piece of dark chocolate or unsweetened cocoa powder (bitter). 2. Have them taste each one. 3. Discuss the different facial expressions they make for each strong taste.
toy_photo: [Image: Spoonful of yogurt and piece of dark chocolate]
activity_photo: [Image: Child tasting a new flavor cautiously]

description: 1. Soak two large bath sponges in warm water and place them on a dry towel on the floor. 2. Take off the child's socks. 3. Let them step on the sponges, feeling the water squish up between their toes.
toy_photo: [Image: Wet bath sponges on a towel]
activity_photo: [Image: Child stepping barefoot on a wet sponge]

description: 1. Have the child sit on the floor. 2. Place a pile of blocks near their left hip. 3. Instruct them to build a tower near their right knee, forcing them to twist and cross their arm over their body for every block.
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching across their body to grab a block]

description: 1. Have the child lay down on the edge of a heavy blanket. 2. Gently roll them up in the blanket like a burrito (leaving their head completely free). 3. Apply gentle, deep pressure squeezes along their body to calm the nervous system.
activity_photo: [Image: Child smiling while rolled up in a blanket]

description: 1. Provide a stiff pipe cleaner and a bowl of O-shaped cereal. 2. Show the child how to hold the pipe cleaner in one hand and a cereal piece in the other. 3. Encourage them to thread the cereal onto the stick to make an edible bracelet.
activity_photo: [Image: Child threading cereal onto a pipe cleaner]

description: 1. Give the child a lump of soft playdough. 2. Show them how to place both hands flat on top of the dough on a table. 3. Guide them to push back and forth to roll the dough into a long 'snake'.
activity_photo: [Image: Child rolling playdough into a long line]

description: 1. Present several snap-together plastic eggs with a tiny toy hidden inside. 2. Have the child hold the egg with both hands. 3. Encourage them to twist and pull the halves apart to find the surprise.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling apart a plastic egg]

description: 1. Give the infant a jumbo cotton ball. 2. Show them how to grasp it with both hands. 3. Encourage them to pull their hands apart to fluff and tear the cotton into wispy clouds.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant pulling a cotton ball apart]

description: 1. Stick two large velcro hair rollers together. 2. Hand the attached rollers to the child. 3. Instruct them to grip one in each hand and pull hard to separate them, listening to the ripping sound.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling two velcro rollers apart]

description: 1. Give the child a child-sized rolling pin and dough. 2. Show them how to grip the handles, one in each hand. 3. Instruct them to push forward and pull backward evenly to flatten the dough.
activity_photo: [Image: Child rolling dough with a rolling pin]

description: 1. Fill a small, easy-to-squeeze plastic bottle with water. 2. Take the child outside to a dry sidewalk. 3. Have them use both hands to squeeze the bottle and spray water to 'paint' the concrete.
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing water onto a sidewalk]

description: 1. Tie a loose knot in a thick piece of rope or a soft scarf. 2. Hand the child the two loose ends. 3. Instruct them to pull both ends outward simultaneously to tighten the knot in the middle.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling two ends of a rope]

description: 1. Give the infant two lightweight plastic blocks. 2. Model the action by clapping your own hands loudly. 3. Guide their hands to bring the blocks together at the midline of their body to make a loud clack.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant banging two blocks together]

description: 1. Provide a large, easy-press craft hole punch (like a star shape) and stiff paper. 2. Have the child insert the paper with one hand. 3. Instruct them to use the palm of their other hand to press the button down firmly.
tools: Large craft hole punch, stiff paper
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing down on a paper punch]

description: 1. Use painter's tape to draw a large figure-eight on the floor. 2. Give the child a toy car. 3. Have them sit in the center and 'drive' the car along the tape, crossing their arm back and forth over their body.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing a car along a figure-eight path]

description: 1. Sit back-to-back with the child on the floor. 2. Hold a ball and twist to your right to hand it to the child. 3. Instruct the child to take it, twist across their body to their left, and hand it back to you on the other side.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent and child passing a ball back-to-back]

description: 1. During bath time, give the child a soapy sponge. 2. Instruct them to hold the sponge in their right hand and scrub their left shoulder and arm. 3. Switch hands to scrub the right arm, crossing the body's midline.
activity_photo: [Image: Child washing their arm with a sponge]

description: 1. Have the child stand with their legs wide apart in a star shape. 2. Demonstrate reaching your right hand down to touch your left toe. 3. Encourage the child to mimic the stretch, crossing their arm entirely across their torso.
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching for opposite toes]

description: 1. Tape a large piece of paper to a wall at chest height. 2. Give the child a marker in their dominant hand. 3. Ask them to draw a long line starting from the far opposite side of their body all the way across to the dominant side.
activity_photo: [Image: Child drawing a long line on wall paper]

description: 1. Sit the infant in a highchair. 2. Place a small, desired snack on the far left corner of the tray. 3. Gently hold their left hand down so they must reach across their body with their right hand to get the food.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant reaching across tray for a snack]

description: 1. Place a pile of blocks on the child's left side and an empty bucket on their right side. 2. Have them sit cross-legged. 3. Instruct them to pick up a block with their right hand by reaching over, and drop it in the right-side bucket.
activity_photo: [Image: Child sorting blocks side to side]

description: 1. Blow bubbles toward the child's left side. 2. Tell them to keep their left hand behind their back. 3. Encourage them to reach across their body with their right hand to pop the bubbles floating on the left.
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching across body to pop a bubble]

description: 1. Place a long toy piano or keyboard in front of the child. 2. Have them use only one pointer finger. 3. Ask them to slide that finger across all the keys from one end to the other, making a continuous sound.
activity_photo: [Image: Child sliding finger across piano keys]

description: 1. Give the child a stick with a ribbon attached (or a scarf). 2. Have them hold it in their right hand. 3. Show them how to wave it from high up on their right side, down to low on their left side, crossing their body.
activity_photo: [Image: Child waving a ribbon diagonally]

description: 1. Lay the infant on their tummy on a soft mat. 2. Shake a highly engaging toy slightly above their eye level. 3. Encourage them to lift their head, chest, and arms off the floor to reach for it, engaging their back extensors.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant lifting chest and arms off the floor]

description: 1. Place a textured, slightly inflated wobble cushion on the floor. 2. Have the child sit on it with their feet flat on the ground. 3. Give them a toy to play with; the unstable seat will force their core to engage to stay upright.
activity_photo: [Image: Child balancing while sitting on a cushion]

description: 1. Have the child tall-kneel (knees on floor, bottom off heels). 2. Hold a balloon or toy slightly above their head. 3. Encourage them to reach up high without sitting back on their heels, forcing core stabilization.
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching up while tall-kneeling]

description: 1. Scatter large sofa pillows across the floor. 2. Ask the child to walk like a bear (hands and feet on the floor, hips high). 3. Have them navigate over the uneven pillows, which demands intense abdominal control.
activity_photo: [Image: Child bear-crawling over cushions]

description: 1. Place a favorite toy on the seat of a soft couch. 2. Sit the child on the floor in front of it. 3. Encourage them to use their arms and core to pull their heavy body up from the soft floor to a standing position.
activity_photo: [Image: Toddler pulling themselves up to stand at a couch]

description: 1. Provide a lightweight medicine ball or a basketball. 2. Have the child sit on the floor with legs in a V. 3. Ask them to place both hands on the ball and push it forcefully across the floor to you.
tools: Heavy ball (basketball or light medicine ball)
activity_photo: [Image: Child forcefully rolling a heavy ball]

description: 1. Lay the infant flat on their back. 2. Hold a tambourine or a soft cushion near their feet. 3. Encourage them to lift their legs into the air and kick the target, building lower abdominal strength.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant kicking up at a tambourine]

description: 1. Have the child lie on their back with knees bent and feet flat. 2. Ask them to lift their bottom off the floor to make a 'bridge'. 3. Roll a toy car under their arched back before they lower themselves down.
activity_photo: [Image: Child lifting hips to let a car roll under]

description: 1. Fill a small plastic sand bucket with a few inches of water. 2. Ask the child to carry the bucket from one side of the patio to the other. 3. The shifting water acts as dynamic weight, forcing their core to constantly adjust.
activity_photo: [Image: Child carefully carrying a bucket of water]

description: 1. Have the child get on their knees on a soft carpet. 2. Tell them to keep their body straight and tall. 3. Challenge them to 'walk' across the room using only their knees, relying entirely on core balance.
activity_photo: [Image: Child walking forward on their knees]

description: 1. Sing a note in a very high pitch, like a mouse. 2. Sing a note in a very low pitch, like a bear. 3. Encourage the infant to babble back, helping them differentiate between starkly contrasting auditory frequencies.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent singing to an attentive infant]

description: 1. Let the child run freely in a safe open area. 2. Blow a soft whistle or ring a bell. 3. Teach them that the specific sound means 'Freeze immediately!', linking a unique auditory cue to a physical action.
activity_photo: [Image: Child freezing mid-run at the sound of a whistle]

description: 1. Turn on a small musical toy or play music from a phone. 2. Hide it under a pillow or behind a curtain while the child covers their eyes. 3. Ask them to follow the sound to locate the hidden object.
activity_photo: [Image: Child listening closely to find a hidden toy]

description: 1. Fill three opaque plastic containers: one with soft cotton, one with rice, one with heavy coins. 2. Shake each one next to the infant's ear. 3. Watch them process the difference between silent, swishy, and clanky sounds.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant listening to a shaking container]

description: 1. Sit facing the child. 2. Clap your hands in a simple pattern: *Clap... Clap-Clap*. 3. Wait and ask the child to repeat the exact auditory rhythm back to you.
activity_photo: [Image: Child mimicking a clapping pattern]

description: 1. Hide a toy cow, pig, and sheep behind your back. 2. Make an animal sound, like 'Baaa'. 3. Bring the toys out and ask the child to point to the animal that makes the sound they just heard.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to a sheep after hearing a baa]

description: 1. Lean in close to the child's ear. 2. Whisper a simple instruction very quietly, such as 'Touch your nose.' 3. See if they can process the low-volume auditory input and execute the action.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent whispering into a child's ear]

description: 1. Set up a bowl of water and an empty metal pot. 2. Give the child small plastic blocks. 3. Have them drop a block into the water (splash) and then into the pot (clang), discussing the different sounds.
tools: Water bowl, metal pot, plastic blocks
toy_photo: [Image: Metal pot and a bowl of water]
activity_photo: [Image: Child dropping a block into a metal pot]

description: 1. Have a family member stand in the hallway out of sight. 2. Have them say 'Hello [Child's Name]!'. 3. Ask the child, 'Who is that?' to help them practice auditory recognition without visual cues.
activity_photo: [Image: Child looking toward a doorway listening]

description: 1. Hold a thick drinking glass securely. 2. Lightly tap the side of the glass with a metal spoon to produce a clear 'ding'. 3. Let the infant tap the glass (while you hold it) to create the resonant sound.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant hitting a glass with a spoon]

description: 1. Tape a large, sturdy stencil (like a star or heart) to a piece of paper. 2. Give the child a thick crayon. 3. Instruct them to follow the inside edge of the stencil to create the shape, linking eye tracking to hand movement.
activity_photo: [Image: Child coloring inside a plastic stencil]

description: 1. Cut a narrow slot in the lid of a plastic tub. 2. Give the child a handful of large, safe plastic coins. 3. Have them visually align the thin edge of the coin with the narrow slot to push it through.
activity_photo: [Image: Child aligning a coin with a slot]

description: 1. Draw two large, distinct dots on a piece of paper, about 6 inches apart. 2. Give the child a marker. 3. Ask them to draw a road connecting one dot directly to the other, requiring them to look ahead to the target.
activity_photo: [Image: Child drawing a line between two dots]

description: 1. Inflate a large balloon. 2. Toss it gently into the air toward the child. 3. The slow descent of the balloon gives their eyes time to track it and tell their hands exactly when to clap together to catch it.
activity_photo: [Image: Child holding arms out to catch a balloon]

description: 1. Provide a stiff shoelace and wooden beads with very large holes. 2. The child must look at the hole, look at the tip of the lace, and guide the tip precisely into the opening.
activity_photo: [Image: Child threading string through a bead]

description: 1. Provide a pegboard and colorful plastic pegs. 2. The child must visually identify an empty hole and guide the peg directly into it, requiring steady hand-eye coordination.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing a peg into a hole]

description: 1. Draw a picture of three blocks stacked (e.g., Red on top of Blue). 2. Give the child the physical blocks. 3. Ask them to look at the 2D drawing and build the 3D tower to match it exactly.
activity_photo: [Image: Child building a tower looking at a picture]

description: 1. Provide a stiff cardboard shape with holes punched around the border and a shoelace. 2. Show the child how to weave the lace 'in and out' of the holes, requiring constant visual tracking of the string's path.
activity_photo: [Image: Child weaving string through a lacing card]

description: 1. Tape a sheet of large bubble wrap to a table. 2. Use a marker to draw a dot on three specific bubbles. 3. Ask the child to visually locate the dotted bubbles and press only those.
toy_photo: [Image: Bubble wrap with dots drawn on it]
activity_photo: [Image: Child pressing a specific marked bubble]

description: 1. Draw a very thick, bold circle on a piece of paper. 2. Give the child a crayon. 3. Ask them to color the 'inside' of the circle, requiring them to use visual boundaries to stop their hand movement.
toy_photo: [Image: Drawing of a thick black circle]
activity_photo: [Image: Child trying to color inside a circle]

description: 1. Have the child lie flat on their back. 2. Place a small stuffed animal on their belly. 3. Instruct them to take a slow, deep breath to make the toy go 'up' and let the air out to make it go 'down', visually teaching deep breathing.
activity_photo: [Image: Child lying down watching a toy on their belly]

description: 1. Provide a firm, squishy stress ball or a balloon filled with flour. 2. When the child is frustrated or overly excited, hand them the ball. 3. Tell them to 'squeeze all your mad out', providing proprioceptive relief.
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing a ball tightly]

description: 1. Hand a fussy infant a sealed clear bottle filled with water, clear glue, and glitter. 2. Shake it vigorously. 3. Let them hold it and watch the glitter slowly settle, which acts as a visually soothing focal point.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant staring at a glitter bottle]

description: 1. When a child needs to redirect aggressive energy, take them to a blank wall. 2. Tell them to put their hands flat and push the wall as hard as they can. 3. This 'heavy work' grounds the nervous system.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing hard against a wall]

description: 1. Lay a heavy blanket on the floor. 2. Have the child lay down and roll them up tightly, leaving their head out. 3. The deep, even pressure mimics a hug and helps calm an overstimulated sensory system.
activity_photo: [Image: Child smiling while wrapped tightly in a blanket]

description: 1. If a child is rushing or frantic at mealtime, place their plate down but hold your hand over it. 2. Say, 'Let's take one big breath first.' 3. Inhale and exhale together, teaching a pause for impulse control.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent and child taking a breath at the table]

description: 1. Before ending a fun activity, set a visual timer (like a sand timer or a color-disappearing clock) for 2 minutes. 2. Say, 'When the red is gone, we clean up.' 3. This helps the child emotionally prepare for transitions.
activity_photo: [Image: Child watching a sand timer]

description: 1. Place a craft feather in the child's open palm. 2. Instruct them to take a breath and blow *very gently* to make it flutter but not fly away. 3. This requires immense breath control and immediate focus.
activity_photo: [Image: Child blowing softly on a feather in their hand]

description: 1. Create a small, dim space with pillows (like under a table or in a small tent). 2. When the child is overwhelmed, invite them to sit in the 'cozy cave'. 3. Let them rest there silently without demands until they are ready to emerge.
tools: Pillows, small tent or blanket fort
activity_photo: [Image: Child resting quietly in a pillow fort]

description: 1. Use a soft, clean makeup brush or sensory brush. 2. Gently and rhythmically stroke the infant's arms, legs, and back. 3. The predictable, soft tactile input can soothe a crying or restless baby.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent brushing an infant's arm]

description: 1. Pour a thin layer of salt or play sand onto a baking tray. 2. Show the child a flashcard with a letter (e.g., 'A'). 3. Guide their pointer finger to trace the shape of the 'A' into the sand, combining tactile and visual learning.
activity_photo: [Image: Child tracing a letter in sand]

description: 1. Sing the 'ABC' song, but purposefully slow down during the 'L-M-N-O-P' section. 2. Enunciate each letter clearly. 3. This prevents the child from thinking 'elemenopee' is a single word and builds phonetic awareness.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent singing slowly to a toddler]

description: 1. Open a large picture book with simple text. 2. As you read out loud, drag your finger directly under the words from left to right. 3. This models the direction of reading and shows that spoken words match printed text.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent pointing to text while reading]

description: 1. Use a puzzle or cards that have uppercase letters separate from lowercase. 2. Give the child the big 'A' and the little 'a'. 3. Explain that they are a 'mommy' letter and a 'baby' letter that belong together.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pairing uppercase and lowercase letters]

description: 1. Write the child's name on a card. Write a completely different name (like 'MOM') on another. 2. Place them on the table. 3. Ask the child, 'Which one is your name?' to build sight recognition of their own identifier.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to their own name card]

description: 1. Sit in front of a mirror with the child. 2. Make an exaggerated 'Mmmmm' sound, pressing your lips together. 3. Point to the child's lips in the mirror and encourage them to make the same shape and sound.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pressing lips together in a mirror]

description: 1. Gather a toy Ball, a toy Bear, and a toy Car. 2. Emphasize the starting sound: 'B-b-ball, B-b-bear, C-c-car'. 3. Ask the child to put the ones that start with 'B-b-b' together in a pile.
activity_photo: [Image: Child grouping a bear and ball together]

description: 1. Give the child paper and a crayon. 2. Tell them to 'write a letter to Grandma'. 3. Praise their random scribbles as writing, teaching them the foundational concept that marks on paper carry communicative meaning.
activity_photo: [Image: Child proudly holding a scribbled paper]

description: 1. Provide safe, food-grade silicone alphabet letters as teethers. 2. As the infant chews on a 'B', say 'You are eating the B! B-b-b!'. 3. This provides early, casual visual exposure to letter shapes during sensory play.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant chewing on a silicone letter]

description: 1. Hide plastic fridge magnet letters in a bin of dry rice. 2. Ask the child to dig them out. 3. As they pull one out, act excited and name the letter out loud to combine sensory play with alphabet recognition.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling a letter out of a rice bin]

description: 1. During diaper changes or bath time, gently wiggle the infant's toes. 2. Count them out loud clearly: 'One, two, three, four, five!'. 3. This introduces the auditory sequence of numbers in a bonding, tactile way.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent touching baby's toes while counting]

description: 1. Gather a mix of large Duplo blocks and small Lego blocks. 2. Set out two bowls. 3. Instruct the child to put the 'Big blocks' here, and the 'Little blocks' there, teaching foundational measurement concepts.
tools: Large and small blocks, two bowls
activity_photo: [Image: Child sorting blocks by size]

description: 1. Place a block with the number '1' and a block with a letter on the table. 2. Hold up one finger and say 'One!'. 3. Ask the child to find the block that shows the number 1.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to a number block]

description: 1. Line up three empty cups. 2. Give the child a handful of crackers. 3. Instruct them to put exactly ONE cracker into each cup, teaching the critical concept of one-to-one correspondence.
activity_photo: [Image: Child placing a single cracker in a cup]

description: 1. Cut a circle and a square out of cardboard. 2. Run the child's finger around the smooth edge of the circle and say 'Round'. 3. Run their finger over the sharp corners of the square and say 'Corners'.
activity_photo: [Image: Child tracing the edge of a shape]

description: 1. Have the child stack exactly three blocks into a tower. 2. Point to the bottom block and say 'One'. 3. Move your finger up and have them say 'Two, Three' to quantify the objects they just built.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent and child counting a block tower]

description: 1. In the bathtub, give the child two cups. 2. Fill one to the brim with water and say 'This is FULL'. 3. Have them pour the water into the other cup until the first one is 'EMPTY', introducing volume concepts.
activity_photo: [Image: Child looking at an empty cup]

description: 1. Provide a large, oversized foam dice. 2. Roll it so the '3' faces up. 3. Take the child's pointer finger and physically touch each dot while counting '1, 2, 3', connecting numbers to physical quantities.
activity_photo: [Image: Child touching dots on a dice]

description: 1. Dump out a box of multi-colored toys. 2. Tell the child, 'Let's find all the RED ones.' 3. Have them pull out every red item and put it in a separate pile, teaching attribute sorting (a pre-math skill).
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling red toys from a pile]

description: 1. Sing songs that involve countdowns, like 'Five Little Monkeys' or 'Ten in the Bed'. 2. Hold up your fingers to represent the monkeys. 3. Put one finger down for each verse, visualizing subtraction.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent holding up fingers while singing]

description: 1. Place two heavy hardcover books into a toddler-sized backpack. 2. Put the backpack on the child and secure the straps. 3. Have them walk around the house; the heavy weight provides organizing joint compression.
activity_photo: [Image: Child walking while wearing a weighted backpack]

description: 1. Provide a small, indoor toddler trampoline with a handlebar. 2. Instruct the child to hold the bar tightly. 3. Encourage them to jump forcefully; the impact of landing provides intense proprioceptive feedback to the legs.
activity_photo: [Image: Child jumping on an indoor trampoline]

description: 1. Lay the infant on their back. 2. Gently hold their ankle and knee. 3. Apply a very soft, rhythmic pulsing pressure, pushing the leg slightly into the hip joint to send calming signals to the nervous system.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent applying gentle compressions to infant's legs]

description: 1. Use a stretchy lycra play tunnel or hold a heavy blanket low over the floor. 2. Have the child crawl through. 3. The resistance of the fabric pushing against their back and limbs provides heavy sensory work.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing through a tight fabric tunnel]

description: 1. Add water to a sandbox to make the sand heavy and dense. 2. Give the child a sturdy plastic shovel. 3. Encourage them to dig a deep hole, forcing them to use intense muscle force to move the heavy material.
activity_photo: [Image: Child exerting effort to dig wet sand]

activity: Pushing a Friend in a Box
description: 1. Have a sibling or a heavy bag of flour sit inside a sturdy cardboard box on a smooth floor. 2. Ask the child to act like a train engine. 3. Have them lean against the box and push it forward using all their strength.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing a heavy box across the floor]

description: 1. Sit on a sofa. 2. Hold the child securely by the hips and let them lay backwards over your lap so their head hangs upside down toward the floor. 3. This changes blood flow and provides strong spatial input.
activity_photo: [Image: Child giggling while hanging upside down off parent's lap]

description: 1. At a playground (when no other kids are waiting), let the child climb UP the plastic slide instead of taking the stairs. 2. The incline forces them to grip tight and pull their body weight up against gravity.
activity_photo: [Image: Child gripping edges to climb up a slide]

description: 1. Place a large mound of tough playdough or kinetic sand on a mat. 2. Take the child's socks off. 3. Encourage them to stand on the dough and stomp to flatten it, sending deep pressure signals through their feet.
tools: Playdough or kinetic sand, floor mat
activity_photo: [Image: Child stomping barefoot on playdough]

description: 1. Give the child a massive, oversized stuffed animal. 2. Tell them to give the bear the biggest, tightest hug they possibly can. 3. The act of squeezing their own arms tightly provides regulating muscle feedback.
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing a giant teddy bear tightly]

description: 1. Sit the child on a low, sturdy rocking horse or rocking toy. 2. Show them how to push with their feet and pull with their hands. 3. The rhythmic back-and-forth motion strongly stimulates the vestibular system.
activity_photo: [Image: Child rocking vigorously on a toy horse]

description: 1. Sit the child securely in a rolling office chair. 2. Hold them safely. 3. Spin the chair slowly 3 times in one direction, pause to let them stabilize, then spin 3 times in the other direction.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent spinning a toddler in a desk chair]

description: 1. Use a safe, secure indoor hammock or a thick blanket held by two adults. 2. Place the infant inside so they are cocooned. 3. Sway them gently in a linear motion (head to toe or side to side) to soothe them.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant swaying gently in a blanket hammock]

description: 1. Lay out a soft gymnastics mat. 2. Have the child crouch down and tuck their chin completely to their chest. 3. Gently guide their hips over to help them roll, safely flipping their head beneath their body.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent helping a child do a forward roll]

description: 1. Provide a curved wooden wobble board. 2. Have the child stand with one foot on each end. 3. Hold their hands while they shift their weight left and right, trying to keep the edges from touching the floor.
activity_photo: [Image: Child shifting weight on a balance board]

description: 1. At a small toddler slide, have the child lay on their tummy facing downward. 2. Hold their sides securely. 3. Let them slide down head-first; this visual and physical shift heavily engages the vestibular system.
activity_photo: [Image: Child sliding down tummy-first]

description: 1. Lay the infant tummy-down on a large yoga ball. 2. Keep a firm grip on their torso. 3. Slowly roll the ball forward so their head dips toward the floor, then roll it back, forcing them to process the tilt.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant balancing on top of a yoga ball]

description: 1. Find a safe, low curb away from traffic. 2. Hold the child's hand. 3. Encourage them to walk like a tightrope walker along the edge, using their arms to balance their center of gravity.
activity_photo: [Image: Child balancing on a curb holding parent's hand]

description: 1. Find a soft, grassy hill with a gentle slope. 2. Have the child lie down sideways at the top with their arms across their chest. 3. Encourage them to roll all the way to the bottom to experience rapid rotary motion.
activity_photo: [Image: Child rolling down a hill laughing]

description: 1. Provide an inflatable hopper ball with a handle. 2. Have the child sit on it and grip the handle. 3. Encourage them to bounce around the room, which requires simultaneous balance, coordination, and motion tracking.
activity_photo: [Image: Child bouncing across the room on a hopper ball]

description: 1. Hand the child a plastic Slinky or coil toy. 2. Show them how to hold one end in the left hand and the other in the right. 3. Encourage them to pull their hands apart to stretch it out, then slowly let it compress back together.
activity_photo: [Image: Child stretching a Slinky with both hands]

description: 1. Provide a set of large, chunky pop beads. 2. Show the child how to line up the peg of one bead with the hole of another. 3. Have them push their hands together firmly to snap the beads into a chain.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing two pop beads together]

description: 1. Give the child a toddler-sized broom. 2. Scatter a few crumpled pieces of paper on the floor. 3. Instruct them to hold the broom with two hands and sweep the paper from the left side of their body over to the right side.
activity_photo: [Image: Child sweeping paper across the floor]

description: 1. Sit facing the child. 2. Lift your right hand and exaggerate tapping your left knee. 3. Tell the child to 'Tap your knee!' and guide their hand across their lap to touch the opposite leg.
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching across lap to tap opposite knee]

description: 1. Lay the infant on their back on a soft mat. 2. Offer your thumbs for them to grasp, wrapping your fingers around their hands. 3. Gently pull their arms forward, encouraging them to engage their neck and abdominal muscles to sit up.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent helping infant pull up to a seated position]

description: 1. Lay on your back and bend your knees so your shins are parallel to the floor. 2. Lift the child and place their tummy resting on your shins. 3. Hold their hands as they balance, engaging their core to 'fly' like an airplane.
activity_photo: [Image: Child balancing on parent's legs flying like an airplane]

description: 1. Give the child a maraca or shaker. 2. Say 'Shake it FAST!' and vigorously shake your own, making a rapid sound. 3. Say 'Shake it sloooow' and make drawn-out, spaced sounds, helping them link physical speed to auditory tempo.
activity_photo: [Image: Child vigorously shaking a maraca]

description: 1. Provide a heavy wooden block and a soft fabric block. 2. Drop the wooden block on a hard floor so it makes a loud 'clack'. 3. Drop the fabric block so it makes no sound. Let the infant repeat this to explore acoustic differences.
toy_photo: [Image: One wood block and one cloth block]
activity_photo: [Image: Infant dropping a wooden block on the floor]

description: 1. Cut a thin, vertical slit in the plastic lid of a coffee can. 2. Give the child a handful of colorful jumbo craft sticks. 3. Have them visually orient the stick vertically to successfully drop it through the narrow slit.
tools: Coffee can with slotted lid, craft sticks
activity_photo: [Image: Child pushing a craft stick through a slot]

description: 1. Lay a long piece of bright painter's tape across the floor in a zig-zag pattern. 2. Dim the lights and give the child a flashlight. 3. Instruct them to make their light beam 'walk' exactly along the tape from start to finish.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing a flashlight at a tape line]

description: 1. Have the child hold up one finger like a candle, and pretend their other hand is holding a flower. 2. Tell them to 'Smell the flower' (deep inhale through the nose). 3. Tell them to 'Blow out the candle' (forceful exhale through the mouth).
activity_photo: [Image: Child pretending to blow out a finger-candle]

description: 1. Have the child lie face down on a soft rug. 2. Take a large, lightweight exercise ball and roll it up and down their back and legs. 3. Apply a firm but gentle downward pressure to provide regulating deep tactile input.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent rolling a yoga ball over a child's back]

description: 1. Write the letters of the child's name in chalk on a chalkboard or driveway. 2. Give the child a wet sponge. 3. Call out a letter (e.g., 'Find the E!') and have them use the sponge to wipe that specific letter away.
activity_photo: [Image: Child wiping chalk off a board with a sponge]

description: 1. Place several large plastic alphabet magnets into a metal baking pan. 2. Ask the child to close their eyes and pick one out. 3. When they open their eyes, enthusiastically announce the letter they 'caught' and its sound.
activity_photo: [Image: Child picking a letter out of a metal pan]

description: 1. Hold up your hands and tell the child you are going to do five high-fives. 2. Have the child slap your hand. 3. Count loudly with each slap ('One! Two! Three! Four! Five!'), connecting physical repetition to numerical sequence.
activity_photo: [Image: Child giving a parent a high five]

description: 1. Provide a pile of plastic counting bears, using only two colors (e.g., Red and Yellow). 2. Set out one red piece of construction paper and one yellow piece. 3. Have the child group the bears onto their matching colored paper.
toy_photo: [Image: Red and yellow plastic counting bears]
activity_photo: [Image: Child placing red bears on red paper]

description: 1. Set up a 'laser maze' by tying yarn back and forth between two chairs, keeping it very low to the ground. 2. Instruct the child to keep their belly flat on the floor. 3. Have them pull themselves forward with their forearms to get under the yarn.
toy_photo: [Image: Red yarn stretched between chair legs]
activity_photo: [Image: Child army crawling on their belly]

description: 1. Tie a thick, soft rope to a heavy laundry basket or a loaded cardboard box. 2. Hand the rope to the child. 3. Encourage them to walk backward while pulling the heavy box across the carpet, engaging heavy work receptors.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling a heavy basket by a rope]

description: 1. Pick the child up securely under their arms and around their chest. 2. Hold them out slightly away from your body. 3. Slowly spin yourself in a circle 2-3 times so the child 'flies' through the air, then stop to let the inner ear settle.
activity_photo: [Image: Parent holding child and spinning in a circle]

description: 1. Sit in a sturdy chair and cross one leg over the other, keeping your foot parallel to the ground. 2. Sit the child on your elevated foot, holding their hands securely. 3. Lift your leg up and down like a gentle elevator ride.
activity_photo: [Image: Child sitting on parent's foot holding hands]

description: 1. Arrange a pillow, a low table, and a cardboard box tunnel in a line. 2. Show the child how to climb over the pillow, crawl under the table, and through the box. 3. Encourage them to navigate the sequence, requiring them to plan multiple body movements.
activity_photo: [Image: Child crawling through a box tunnel]

description: 1. Place 3 hula hoops flat on the ground in a row. 2. Show the child how to step inside the first hoop, then the next. 3. Encourage them to step carefully into each one without tripping on the edges.
activity_photo: [Image: Child stepping carefully into a hoop]

description: 1. Stand facing the child. 2. Strike a distinct, simple pose (e.g., both hands on your head). 3. Ask the child to make their body look exactly like yours.
toy_photo: [Image: Icon of a stick figure posing]
activity_photo: [Image: Child copying parent with hands on head]

description: 1. Prop a sturdy piece of cardboard across two stacks of books to make a low bridge. 2. Give the child a toy car. 3. Have them figure out how to crouch down to push the car all the way under the bridge without knocking it over.
toy_photo: [Image: Toy car and a cardboard bridge]
activity_photo: [Image: Child crouching to push a car under a bridge]

description: 1. Stack three sofa cushions to make a 'mountain'. 2. Place a favorite toy on the peak. 3. Let the infant figure out how to coordinate their arms and legs to scale the soft, unstable obstacle.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant climbing over stacked cushions]

description: 1. Place a wide laundry basket about three feet away from the child. 2. Give them several soft plush balls or rolled-up socks. 3. Have them practice the sequence of winding back their arm and releasing the item toward the target.
activity_photo: [Image: Child throwing a soft ball into a basket]

description: 1. Place a large, light ball directly in front of the child's feet. 2. Stand a few steps away. 3. Instruct them to swing their leg to kick the ball to you, helping them plan the timing and force of a lower-body action.
activity_photo: [Image: Child swinging foot to kick a ball]

description: 1. Place a 6-foot strip of bright painter's tape in a straight line on the floor. 2. Ask the child to walk from one end to the other, keeping both feet directly on the tape the entire time.
toy_photo: [Image: Bright colored tape on the floor]
activity_photo: [Image: Child carefully walking along a tape line]

description: 1. When the infant is crawling, place a gentle barrier (like a pillow or your arm) directly in front of them. 2. Call to them from behind. 3. Encourage them to figure out how to put their crawling motion into reverse.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant pushing backward on hands and knees]

description: 1. Set up 4 or 5 plastic cones (or tall plastic cups) in a zig-zag pattern. 2. Show the child how to weave around them like a snake. 3. Encourage them to walk the path without knocking any over.
activity_photo: [Image: Child walking in a zig-zag around cones]

description: 1. Give the child a doll or a teddy bear. 2. Say, 'Show me the baby's nose!' 3. Wait for the child to point to the correct body part on the toy, demonstrating their comprehension of spoken words.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to a doll's nose]

description: 1. Give a single, clear instruction like, 'Give me the ball.' 2. Hold your hand out expectantly. 3. Wait up to 10 seconds for the child to process the language and hand over the item.
activity_photo: [Image: Child handing a ball to an adult]

description: 1. Point to a shelf with several familiar books. 2. Ask the child, 'Can you bring me the book about the dog?' 3. Have them scan the options, recall the content based on your words, and bring it to you.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling a specific book off a shelf]

description: 1. Show the child a photo containing multiple family members. 2. Ask, 'Where is Grandpa?' 3. Watch the child scan the faces and point to the correct person.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to a face in a photo]

description: 1. When someone is leaving the room, say 'Wave bye-bye!' clearly, but do not wave your own hand. 2. See if the infant understands the verbal cue alone and raises their hand to wave.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant waving independently upon hearing a cue]

description: 1. Let the child run or walk away from you in a safe space. 2. Say 'Stop!' in a firm, clear voice. 3. Praise them heavily when they halt their body upon hearing the auditory command.
activity_photo: [Image: Child freezing mid-step upon hearing 'Stop']

description: 1. Sit in a room with the child. 2. Say, 'Point to the ceiling!' and wait for them to point up. 3. Say, 'Point to the floor!' and wait for them to point down, teaching spatial vocabulary.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing up at the ceiling]

description: 1. Before going outside, say 'Go get your shoes.' 2. Wait for the child to process the request, walk to where their shoes are kept, and bring them back to you.
activity_photo: [Image: Child carrying their shoes toward parent]

description: 1. When a distinct sound happens outside (e.g., a siren, a dog barking), say, 'Listen! What is that?' 2. Give them a moment to answer, or provide the answer ('It's a dog!'). 3. Help them associate words with environmental noises.
activity_photo: [Image: Child looking surprised at a loud noise]

description: 1. Hold up a ball and a block. 2. Ask the infant, 'Where is the block?' 3. Watch their eyes or hands to see if they turn their attention to the correct object named.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant staring at the block when asked]

description: 1. During a meal, when the child finishes a bite, tap your fingertips together and say 'More'. 2. Wait for the child to attempt to mimic the sign or sound to request additional food.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant tapping fingers together for more food]

description: 1. Hand the child a toy car or airplane. 2. Demonstrate making a 'Vroom' or 'Zoom' sound while playing with it. 3. Encourage the child to vocalize their own sound effects during imaginative play.
activity_photo: [Image: Child making a 'vroom' face while pushing a toy car]

description: 1. Hold up a cracker and a slice of apple. 2. Ask, 'Do you want the cracker or the apple?' 3. Wait for the child to attempt to say the name of the desired item rather than just pointing.
activity_photo: [Image: Child vocalizing their snack choice]

description: 1. Sing a very familiar song like 'Old MacDonald'. 2. Pause before the animal sound: 'And on that farm he had a cow, E-I-E-I-O, with a...' 3. Wait for the child to shout 'Moo!' to complete the phrase.
activity_photo: [Image: Child enthusiastically shouting a song lyric]

description: 1. When a toy accidentally drops or falls over, throw your hands up and say 'Uh-oh!'. 2. Repeat this consistently. 3. Watch for the child to begin using 'Uh-oh' independently when they drop something.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant saying 'uh-oh' after dropping a toy]

description: 1. When the family dog or cat is in the other room, say, 'Let's call the dog.' 2. Call the pet's name loudly. 3. Have the child use their loud voice to yell the pet's name, practicing volume and pronunciation.
activity_photo: [Image: Child yelling for a pet]

description: 1. When the child raises their arms to be picked up, pause. 2. Say, 'Up?' 3. Wait for them to vocalize the word 'Up' or make a sound resembling it before lifting them, rewarding their expressive effort.
activity_photo: [Image: Child with arms raised saying 'Up']

description: 1. Hide several familiar objects (a ball, a spoon, a toy car) in a bin of rice. 2. As the child digs one out, excitedly ask, 'What did you find?!' 3. Have them name the object aloud.
toy_photo: [Image: Bin of rice with hidden toys]
activity_photo: [Image: Child proudly holding up and naming a toy spoon]

description: 1. Ask the child a question you know the answer to is no (e.g., 'Do you want a nap?'). 2. Exaggerate shaking your head side to side and say 'No'. 3. Encourage them to shake their head to express refusal non-verbally.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant shaking head no]

description: 1. Place a highly desired toy on a shelf where the infant can see it but not reach it. 2. Wait for them to extend their arm and point their index finger toward the toy to initiate communication with you.
toy_photo: [Image: Toy placed high on a shelf]
activity_photo: [Image: Infant pointing insistently at an out-of-reach toy]

description: 1. Show the infant a bright toy. 2. Place it on the floor and cover it completely with a small blanket while they watch. 3. Ask 'Where did it go?' and let them pull the blanket off to reveal it.
activity_photo: [Image: Infant pulling a blanket off a hidden toy]

description: 1. Tape a paper towel tube vertically to a wall. 2. Have the child drop a small ball into the top. 3. They will learn that even though the ball disappears inside the tube, it still exists and will come out the bottom.
activity_photo: [Image: Child watching a ball fall out of a tube]

description: 1. Drape a lightweight towel or blanket over the child's head. 2. Say, 'Where is [Child's Name]?' 3. Wait for them to pull the towel off and shout 'Here I am!', understanding they didn't disappear.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pulling a towel off their head]

description: 1. Place a small toy under one of three identical opaque plastic cups. 2. Slowly mix the cups around on the table. 3. Ask the child to point to the cup hiding the toy, tracking it with their eyes.
toy_photo: [Image: Three plastic cups and a small ball]
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to a cup hiding a toy]

description: 1. Open a low, safe drawer. 2. Have the child put a toy inside and push the drawer closed. 3. Ask, 'Where is the toy?' and encourage them to open the drawer again to retrieve it.
activity_photo: [Image: Child opening a drawer to find a toy]

description: 1. Hide a phone or a toy that makes continuous noise under a sofa cushion. 2. Turn the sound on. 3. Ask the child to find the noise, teaching them that objects making sound out of sight still exist.
activity_photo: [Image: Child lifting a cushion to find a ringing phone]

activity: Hide and Seek Behind a Door
description: 1. Walk behind an open door so the child cannot see you. 2. Call their name. 3. Wait for them to walk around the door to find you, reinforcing that you exist even when out of view.
activity_photo: [Image: Child peeking around a door to find a parent]

description: 1. Give the child a shape sorter bucket. 2. Have them push all the blocks through the holes. 3. Show them how to remove the lid to retrieve the blocks, showing the blocks didn't vanish inside.
activity_photo: [Image: Child opening the lid of a shape sorter to get blocks]

description: 1. Put several toys into a box with an opaque lid. 2. Put the lid on. 3. Ask the child to get a specific toy from the box, requiring them to know the toys are still in there.
toy_photo: [Image: Plastic storage bin with a lid]
activity_photo: [Image: Child taking the lid off a bin to get a toy]

description: 1. Use a cardboard tube or a play tunnel. 2. Push a toy car into one end so it disappears. 3. Have the child wait at the other end for the car to emerge, trusting that it will travel through.
activity_photo: [Image: Child waiting at the end of a tube for a car]

activity: Cheerios in an Ice Cube Tray
description: 1. Place one Cheerio or small puff in each compartment of a clean, empty ice cube tray. 2. Encourage the child to use their thumb and index finger to pluck the cereal out one by one.
tools: Ice cube tray, Cheerios or puffs
activity_photo: [Image: Child pinching a puff out of a tray]

description: 1. Give the child a sheet of small, round stickers (like garage sale price tags). 2. Peel back the edge of the sticker sheet slightly. 3. Have the child pinch the tiny sticker to remove it and place it on a piece of paper.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pinching a small sticker off a sheet]

activity: Pulling Pipe Cleaners from a Colander
description: 1. Turn a kitchen colander upside down. 2. Thread several pipe cleaners half-way through the holes so they stick out like spikes. 3. Have the child pinch the tips and pull them all out.
toy_photo: [Image: Metal colander with fuzzy pipe cleaners sticking out]
activity_photo: [Image: Child pinching a pipe cleaner to pull it out]

description: 1. Cut a piece of yarn into several 1-inch pieces. 2. Scatter them on a contrasting colored table or floor. 3. Ask the child to pick up the tiny pieces of string, requiring precise fingertip coordination.
activity_photo: [Image: Child carefully pinching a piece of string]

description: 1. Form a large ball of playdough. 2. Show the child how to use their thumb and pointer finger to pinch the dough like a crab. 3. Have them pinch off tiny pieces until the whole ball is broken down.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pinching off pieces of playdough]

description: 1. Provide an empty plastic water bottle with a small opening. 2. Place a bowl of dry kidney beans next to it. 3. Instruct the child to pinch one bean at a time and drop it into the narrow hole.
toy_photo: [Image: Plastic water bottle and dry beans]
activity_photo: [Image: Child dropping a bean into a bottle]

description: 1. Give the child a magazine or a book with standard, thin paper pages (not a board book). 2. Show them how to pinch the top corner of the page gently to turn it without ripping it.
activity_photo: [Image: Child carefully pinching a page to turn it]

description: 1. Place a half-empty box of facial tissues in front of the infant. 2. Pull the first tissue up slightly. 3. Encourage the infant to pinch the tissue and pull it all the way out (supervise so they don't eat it).
toy_photo: [Image: Tissue box with a tissue popping up]
activity_photo: [Image: Infant pinching a tissue to pull it out]

description: 1. Give the child a small, easy-to-squeeze wooden clothespin. 2. Show them how to pinch the top ends together to open the 'mouth'. 3. Have them clip the clothespin onto the edge of a sturdy paper plate.
activity_photo: [Image: Child squeezing a clothespin onto a plate]

description: 1. Scatter a few large pieces of fuzz or cotton fluff on a dark carpet. 2. Tell the child they are a 'vacuum cleaner'. 3. Have them crawl around and use their thumb and pointer finger to pick up the fuzz.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pinching a piece of fuzz off the floor]

description: 1. Gather a mix of adult-sized socks and toddler-sized socks. 2. Place them in a laundry basket. 3. Have the child sort the socks into two piles: 'Big Socks' and 'Little Socks', learning to distinguish size.
toy_photo: [Image: One large adult sock and one tiny baby sock]
activity_photo: [Image: Child sorting socks into two piles]

description: 1. Create a pile of 10 blue blocks and 1 red block. 2. Ask the child, 'Can you find the red block?' 3. They must visually scan the pile to isolate the single item that is a different color.
toy_photo: [Image: Pile of blue blocks with one red one]
activity_photo: [Image: Child picking the red block out of the blue pile]

description: 1. Lay two pairs of matching picture cards face up on the table (e.g., two cats, two dogs). 2. Hand the child a dog card. 3. Ask them to place it on top of the card that looks exactly the same.
activity_photo: [Image: Child placing a card on its identical match]

activity: Putting All Circles in a Pile
description: 1. Cut out several shapes (circles, squares, triangles) from cardboard. 2. Lay them on the floor. 3. Tell the child, 'Find all the round circles' and have them collect only that specific shape.
activity_photo: [Image: Child grabbing only the circle shapes]

description: 1. Place a bright, contrasting sticker somewhere obvious in the room (like on a white door). 2. Tell the child, 'There is a sticker hiding in this room! Can you see it with your eyes?' 3. Let them scan the environment.
activity_photo: [Image: Child pointing to a sticker on the wall]

description: 1. Place the child's cup next to an adult's cup or a sibling's cup on the table. 2. Say, 'Which cup is yours?' 3. The child must distinguish their personal item based on visual characteristics like color or size.
tools: Child's cup and an adult's cup
toy_photo: [Image: Small sippy cup next to a large mug]
activity_photo: [Image: Child reaching for their specific cup]

description: 1. Create a pile of mixed-up family shoes. 2. Hand the child one of their own shoes. 3. Say, 'Can you find the other shoe that matches this one?'
